You use the participle constructions of written French: ayant terminé, étant arrivés, le contrat signé, une fois installés, to link actions in a concise style.
Having signed the contract, Julien started on 1 July.
Having arrived late, we didn’t see the mayor.
The contract signed, he called Ioana.
Once settled in, we visited the hall.
On arriving in Lille, the team got a poor reception.
To form the perfect participle: ayant + participle, étant + participle.
To express prior action or cause with a participle clause: Ayant fini, il est parti.
To use the absolute participle clause: Le travail terminé, nous sommes sortis.
To use the appositive past participle: Arrivés à Lille, ils… / Une fois installés, …
To recognise these constructions in reports, articles and literature.

Friday, 25 July 2030. Julien has been working for three weeks at the new office of the “Musique en partage” network, in the Croix-Rousse. His assistant, Amina Diallo, helps him draft his first report for the ministry. Julien dictates, Amina corrects.
Right. I’ll write: “We went to Lille on 8 July. When we arrived, the mayor wasn’t there.”
That’s correct, but for a report it’s a bit long. We could write: “Having arrived in Lille on 8 July, we noted the mayor’s absence.”
“Having arrived in Lille…” That’s more elegant. Next: “As we didn’t have an appointment, we went straight to the school.”
“Not having an appointment, we proceeded directly to the school.” The present participle replaces “comme”.
OK. And at the school, the director was suspicious. She had read the Lyon Vérité article, last year’s. She thought the project cost too much.
Then: “Having read an erroneous article published in 2029, the director was initially reluctant.” You see? “Ayant lu” shows that the reading happened before.
But I showed her the La Duchère video. And when she saw the children playing in the dark, she changed her mind.
“The video viewed, the director changed her mind.” That’s an absolute participle clause: a noun, a participle, a comma.
It sounds like Flaubert. And Strasbourg? There it was the opposite. The mayor was waiting for us at the station with a brass band.
“Welcomed at the station by the mayor and a municipal brass band, we immediately visited the proposed premises.” Once the premises had been visited, what did we do?
We ate an enormous choucroute. But we’re not putting that in the report.
(laughs) No. We write: “The visit over, a working lunch made it possible to address budgetary questions.”
Amina, you’re a genius. With you, even a choucroute becomes a ministerial report.
It is formed with “ayant” or “étant” + the past participle. It expresses an action COMPLETED before another, often with a nuance of cause:
Ayant signé le contrat, il a commencé.
Après avoir signé… / Comme il avait signé…
Étant arrivés tard, nous n’avons pas vu le maire.
N’ayant pas de rendez-vous, nous sommes partis.
The subject of the participle must be the SAME as that of the main verb. “Ayant fini, il est parti” = he finished and he left.
A noun with its own participle, set off by a comma. Its subject is DIFFERENT from that of the main verb. Very common in written style:
The contract signed, Julien called Ioana.
The video viewed, the director changed her mind.
The visit over, we went to lunch.
The sun having set, the children went inside.
English has the same construction (“The contract signed, …”), but it sounds more literary. In French it is elegant, not pretentious.
The past participle alone at the start of a sentence agrees with the subject of the main verb:
Arrivés à Lille, nous avons constaté l’absence du maire.
Accueillis par le maire, nous avons visité le local.
Une fois installés, nous avons commencé.
The classic mistake (in French too!): “Arrivé à la gare, le train était parti.” ✗ — it sounds as if the train arrived at the station. Correct: “Arrivé à la gare, j’ai vu que le train était parti.”
Quand on est arrivés, … / Comme on n’avait pas…
Après être arrivés, … / Une fois arrivés, …
Arrivés à…, / Ayant constaté…, / La visite terminée, …
In speech, participle constructions sound “bookish”. You’ll hear them on the news, in speeches, at conferences, but rarely among friends.
Not having an appointment, we went to the school.
Having arrived in Lille, we noted the mayor’s absence.
“Ayant lu l’article, elle était réticente.” What happened first?
Arrivé à la gare, j’ai vu le train.
Arrivé à la gare, le train était parti.
“Étant partis tôt” — which auxiliary does “partir” take?
In which register do you use “La visite terminée, …”?
Où se trouve le nouveau bureau de Julien ?
Pourquoi la directrice de Lille était-elle méfiante ?
Elle avait lu un article erroné
Qui attendait Julien à la gare de Strasbourg ?
Not having an appointment, we went straight to the school.
The absolute participle clause has a subject that is…
the same as the main verb’s
Welcomed at the station by the mayor, we visited the premises.

On Tuesday 1 July, at eight in the morning, Julien pushed open the door of his new office for the first time. It was a former silk workshop, on the third floor of a building in the Croix-Rousse, with very high windows built long ago to let in the light the weavers needed. Ioana’s firm had renovated it in a month. Radu had supervised the work.

In the middle of the room was a long wooden table, worn, covered in marks. Radu had found it in the building’s cellar. According to the old caretaker, it was the table at which the last canut of the house had worked, in the fifties. Julien decided to make it his desk. He put three things on it: his notebook, Sami’s drawing and a photo of Hélène on her bench.

At a quarter past eight his assistant arrived. Amina Diallo was thirty-one. Born in Dakar, arrived in Villeurbanne at the age of six, she had worked for eight years in the administration of the Opéra de Lyon. She spoke fast, wrote even faster, and had a rule she announced to Julien on the very first day: “In a report, Mr Moreau, there are no emotions. There are facts.”

Julien soon realised he would never win an argument with Amina. The first week, having spent his days on the phone with the ten partner cities, he came home with a headache and a hoarse voice. He hated spreadsheets, budgets and forms. Amina loved them. They were, according to Ioana, the most mismatched and the most efficient team in France.

On 8 July they took the TGV to Lille. It was raining. Having arrived at the town hall without an appointment, because of a secretarial error, they learned that the mayor was on holiday. Having nothing else to do, they went straight to the music school in the Moulins district, where the future orchestra was to be born. The director, Mrs Vandamme, received them coldly.

The year before she had read the Lyon Vérité article, shared at the time on social media all over France. She was convinced the project was a waste of public money. Julien didn’t argue. He took out his phone and showed her Mrs Mansouri’s video: the La Duchère children playing the waltz in the dark, during the power cut.

The video over, Mrs Vandamme sat silent for a long time. Then she asked if she could watch it again. She watched it three times. The third time, she took out a handkerchief. “Forgive me,” she said. “My father was a miner. He played the cornet in the mine’s brass band. I hadn’t thought about it in forty years.” An hour later she signed the agreement.

On the train home, Amina wrote up the minutes of the visit. Julien read them over her shoulder. There wasn’t a word about Mrs Vandamme’s father, or the handkerchief, or the mine’s brass band. There was only: “The video viewed, the director proved favourable.” Julien found it terribly sad. Amina found it perfect.

In Strasbourg, on 15 July, everything had been exactly the opposite: welcomed on the station platform by the mayor, Mrs Keller, and by the full municipal brass band, they crossed the city to music all the way to the town hall. Passers-by stopped to applaud without knowing why. Julien felt like a Roman general.

Mrs Keller had already chosen the premises: a former deconsecrated chapel on the banks of the Ill, with extraordinary acoustics. The visit over, she took them to lunch in a winstub, where they were served a choucroute big enough to feed an entire orchestra. At dessert, a little girl, the cook’s daughter, came up to Julien. “Are you the waltz man?”

Julien understood that day that the story of the waltz had travelled faster than he had. Children all over France had seen the video, read the articles, heard the concert on the radio. They didn’t necessarily know who Hélène or Henri were. But they knew that somewhere there was a waltz children played in the dark, and they wanted to play it too.

In Marseille, on 22 July, it was thirty-four degrees. The Estaque music school was a little yellow house above the harbour, with a view over the whole bay. Its director, Mr Benhamou, was a tall white-haired man, a former jazz saxophonist who had played in Paris clubs in the eighties before coming back to the neighbourhood where he was born.

Having grown up in those very streets himself, he needed no explanations. “When I was ten,” he said, “nobody gave me an instrument. I stole my first saxophone. I don’t recommend it to anyone.” Once the neighbourhood children had gathered in the courtyard, about twenty of them, he took out his saxophone and played, without a score, the first three notes of the waltz.

Julien froze. “You know it?” Mr Benhamou smiled. “Everybody knows it here. The kids learned it listening to the radio.” Then he took him to the back of the courtyard, where a patch of earth was waiting in the sun, facing the sea. “Your lime tree will go here. It’ll have the best view in France. As long as it can stand the mistral.”

That evening Julien called Ioana from the Estaque harbour. He told her about the saxophone, the courtyard, the view. In the distance, across the bay, you could make out the white rocks of Les Goudes, where his grandparents’ house with the blue shutters stood. “The first lime tree will be planted a few kilometres from the terrace where my grandmother used to dance,” he said. “Do you think that’s a coincidence?”

Ioana answered that she had stopped believing in coincidences long ago. She was three months pregnant. The nausea had passed. On 30 July, at the scan, the doctor showed them on the screen a tiny heart beating very fast. He asked whether they wanted to know the baby’s sex. They looked at each other and answered no at the same time.

Rose-Hélène, for her part, had no doubt. The baby was called “Baby Waltz”, and he would play the harmonica. She had started talking to her mother’s belly every evening before bed, very seriously. She told it about her day, the pigeons in the square, Odile’s cat. Then she blew three notes on Henri’s harmonica, very close to the belly, “so he learns”.

Meanwhile, in the big greenhouse in the Parc de la Tête d’Or, Odile spent her mornings with Mr Fournier. The twelve little lime trees were waiting, lined up in their pots, now more than a metre tall. Odile had insisted on writing the labels herself. On each was the name of a city and, underneath, always the same words: “Henri and Hélène, 1962”.

Mr Fournier taught her to water the young trees, check their leaves, protect them from strong sun. Odile took notes in a little notebook, as seriously as Amina did her reports. One August morning, bending down to read a label, she slipped and sprained her wrist. Dr Martin put a splint on it. She kept coming anyway.

At the beginning of August, Théo got his baccalauréat results. Highest honours. His mother called Julien at seven in the morning, crying with joy, to tell him the news before she had even called her own sister. Théo just sent a three-word message: “I am ready.” He was starting at the Conservatoire in September, in the conducting class.

Radu and Lucia moved in August into a small flat in La Duchère, five minutes from the Hélène Morel hall. It was Lucia who wanted it. “If I have to get sixty children dancing three days a week,” she said, “I want to be able to walk there.” Radu didn’t argue. Since their wedding he had learned that arguing with Lucia was a delightful but useless waste of time.

On Wednesday 3 September, the La Duchère orchestra resumed rehearsals. For the first time it wasn’t Julien conducting, but Théo, with Lucia at his side. Julien had promised not to come, so as not to make the young conductor nervous. He kept his promise for exactly forty minutes. Then he took the bus to La Duchère.

Having arrived at the hall, he found Sami’s father sitting on a chair next to the half-open door. Since the Paris trip he had become the rehearsals’ volunteer guard. He saw Julien arrive, put a finger to his lips, and motioned him to hide behind the door. From there you could see everything without being seen.

What Julien saw worried him at first. The children were testing their new conductor, as children test all new conductors. Yanis was pulling faces behind his cello. The second violins were chatting. A boy dropped his flute three times, on purpose. Théo, in the middle, red to the ears, was trying to start the Brahms dance. Nobody was listening to him.

It was Lucia who reacted first. Without a word, she began to stamp her foot, slowly, then faster, then faster still. The children fell silent one by one, surprised. After a minute the whole hall was stamping with her, in rhythm. Then Lucia stopped dead, and in the silence that followed, she held out her hand towards Théo, as you introduce an artist.

Théo understood. He didn’t raise his baton. He sat down at the piano, at the back of the hall, and played, very softly, the first three notes of Henri’s waltz. Then he stopped. He waited. And Inès, in the front row, raised her clarinet and played the next three notes. Then Yanis, on the cello. Then the whole orchestra.

Behind the door, Julien felt his eyes sting. Sami’s father winked at him. Julien left on tiptoe, without being seen, and took the bus back to the Croix-Rousse. On the bus he wrote in his notebook: “3 September. I am no longer needed. It is the finest day of my career.”

That evening Théo called him, in despair. “It was a disaster,” he said. “They didn’t listen to me. Without Lucia I’d have stopped everything.” Julien let him talk. Then he told him about his own first rehearsal, fifteen years earlier, in a school in Villeurbanne. A child had thrown an eraser that hit him on the forehead. He nearly resigned that very evening.

“And the waltz?” Julien asked. “How was the waltz?” Théo hesitated. “The waltz… was good. Very good, even. They played it without me. I didn’t do anything.” Julien smiled, alone in his kitchen. “Théo, that’s exactly what conducting is. The day they play without you means you’ve done your job.” Théo said nothing. But Julien heard him breathe, relieved.

In September, Julien and Amina visited the last three cities: Toulouse, Nantes and Clermont-Ferrand. In Toulouse the welcome was warm. In Nantes a former shipyard was proposed as a rehearsal hall. In Clermont-Ferrand, on the other hand, the mayor was cautious: the city had budget problems. He promised to give his answer in November.

At the end of the month, Amina wrote the first official report. Julien read it twice, looking for an emotion, any emotion. There wasn’t one. Then he reached the last sentence: “Everywhere the team went, the children asked the same question: ‘Will we play the waltz?’” He looked up at Amina.

“I thought there were no emotions in a report.” Amina shrugged, without taking her eyes off her screen. “It isn’t an emotion, Mr Moreau. It’s a fact. I heard it sixty-seven times. I counted.” Julien laughed. He was beginning to understand that, beneath her spreadsheets and rules, Amina had a heart as big as his own.

On 29 September Catherine Dumas called. The report had been read by the minister himself, who had asked to attend the first planting, in Marseille, on Saturday 11 October. Amina immediately opened a new spreadsheet entitled “Ministerial visit”. Julien immediately got a headache.

That same evening, at home, something more important than a ministerial visit happened. Rose-Hélène, as every evening, blew her three notes on the harmonica, right next to her mother’s belly. And Ioana let out a little cry. She took Julien’s hand and put it on her belly. Under his fingers, something moved. Once. Then a second time.

“He heard,” Rose-Hélène whispered, very proud. “Baby Waltz heard.” Julien remembered another evening, two and a half years earlier, when Rose-Hélène herself had given her first kick while he was singing a lullaby. Some things in this family seemed to repeat themselves like the verses of a waltz.

On Friday 10 October, the day before leaving for Marseille, Odile packed her bag carefully. She put in a dress, a shawl, her medicines, her splint and a bottle of water. Then she went to the greenhouse with Mr Fournier to fetch the first of the twelve lime trees. The label read: “Marseille. Henri and Hélène, 1962.”

She refused to let it travel in the instrument van. “It’s coming on the train, with me,” she decided. “On my lap. Henri never travelled in a van, and his grandson isn’t going to start.” Nobody dared point out to her that a lime tree was nobody’s grandson. Or perhaps it was, after all.

That evening, before going to bed, Julien looked at the big map of France Amina had pinned to the office wall. Ten red pins marked the ten cities. An eleventh, a golden one, marked Lyon. On his phone a message from Amina had just arrived: “Report sent. All emotions deleted. Except the last sentence. Have a good trip.” Julien switched off the light, smiling.

Having taken up his duties on 1 July 2030, the national coordinator moved into premises in the Croix-Rousse, a former silk workshop renovated by the Atelier Rhône firm. The work completed, the team was able to begin its tour of the partner cities.

Arriving in Lille on 8 July, the team initially met with reluctance. Not having been informed directly about the project, the director of the music school feared it would cost too much. The La Duchère video viewed, she proved favourable.

Welcomed in Strasbourg on 15 July by the mayor in person, the team visited three possible premises. The choice made, a working lunch made it possible to address budgetary questions. The city undertook to fund half of the project.

In Marseille, on 22 July, the team was received at the Estaque school by its director, Mr Benhamou, a former jazz musician. Having grown up in the neighbourhood himself, he immediately understood the value of the project. Once the children had gathered, a first rehearsal took place that very day.

Consequently, seven cities out of ten have given their final agreement. The other three, not yet having designated premises, will be visited in September. The planting of the lime trees, scheduled from October, will be coordinated by Mrs Odile Bernard, volunteer.

The coordinator wishes to stress that, everywhere the team went, the children asked the same question: “Will we play the waltz?” The answer having been yes each time, the children’s agreement, for its part, is unanimous.
